item.title: Different problems build different skills
item.description: I’ve been thinking about why I’d point students in a programming course toward both the International Collegiate Programming Contest (ICPC) and Kaggle. I can picture a room scheduling problem on either one. A programming contest might give me a list of events and ask how many rooms they need. A Kaggle prediction challenge might give me past records and ask how busy those rooms will be next week. I’d be curious about a different part of each problem.

item.title: Moving from practice to real work
item.description: When I think about what students can get from research or an internship, I picture a small task that gives them a view of the bigger work. Say a student joins a faculty research group and helps summarize survey responses from a study that follows people over a semester. At a group meeting, someone asks whether the people who skipped the last survey were different from those who completed it. The student can compare their earlier answers, bring back what they found, and hear how it changes what the group is willing to claim.

item.title: Problem solving still needs fundamentals
item.description: If someone asked me whether a campus shuttle had become more reliable, I’d probably start with how late it usually runs. Then I think about a rider who misses the same connection every Tuesday. The shuttle could improve its average by running closer to schedule at quieter times, and that rider would still spend Tuesday waiting for the next bus. I’d want to know what changed for that rider before I called the new schedule an improvement.

item.title: Congratulations to our UWF ICPC teams
item.description:
On Saturday, November 7, two teams from the University of West Florida competed in Division 2 at the ICPC Southeast Regional at Florida State University in Tallahassee. One of our teams solved eight problems, placing first in Division 2 at the FSU site and fourth in Division 2 across the Southeast region. Our other team solved three problems. Congratulations to both teams for representing UWF! UWF contest recap

Even if you’ve never competed, I think these problems are worth a look. Often the interesting part comes before you write any code. You have to figure out what the problem is asking, decide which details matter, and look for a small example that might break your first idea. That kind of problem solving and critical thinking comes up in technical interviews, especially when you’re asked to explain why you chose an approach and how you know it works.

item.title: Grow with your AI agent skills
item.description:
Suppose I have a year’s worth of electricity bills and want to see how my usage changed. I could ask an AI assistant to pull the billing dates, electricity use, and current charges into a table. The first few rows might look fine. Then one month shows an unusually high charge, and I realize the assistant copied the amount due, which includes a balance from the previous month.

That distinction is worth saving in an agent skill, a set of instructions an AI assistant can reuse for a particular kind of work. For the next batch, I’d tell it which line on the bill to use for current charges and ask it to flag values it can’t locate. It could also put dates in a consistent format, keep a reference to the source page for each row, and leave names, addresses, and account numbers out of the table.

item.title: What Git helps me remember
item.description:
I appreciate Git most when something was working yesterday and I can’t remember what I changed. I might have a guess, but looking at the last version that worked gives me something concrete to go on. I can see what changed and sometimes find a clue in a file I hadn’t even thought to check. Pro Git’s introduction to version control

I like having that option when I write, too. Say I cut a paragraph from a report and realize a week later that it had the clearest explanation. I can bring back the paragraph and keep the edits I made since. I also like finding a note about what I was thinking at the time. “Reorganize the results around the two main findings” might remind me why I moved things around. A name like report-final-v3 mostly tells me I thought I was finished.

item.title: Why I keep my notes in Markdown and Obsidian
item.description: I like being able to open a note and read it right away. With Markdown, I can see where a section starts, what belongs in a list, and where a link goes, even in a plain text editor. A line starting with ## is a heading. That little bit of structure is enough for most of what I write down. If you’re curious about the syntax, CommonMark has a short tutorial you can open in your browser. CommonMark’s Markdown tutorial

item.title: Why I like keeping a work log
item.description:
The hardest part of switching between projects is often remembering where I left off. A few days later, I might remember that I tried something and that it worked. The part I actually need is what I changed and why I stopped there.

A good log entry can be two sentences. “Lowering the batch size stopped the crash. I still need to see how much slower it runs.” That’s enough to pick up the work without repeating the experiment or rereading a long chat. When I have several things going at once, I find it easier to leave a line like that before switching projects than to reconstruct the whole day later.
